results.claim: Exact stationary rarity. For 0<p<1, put α=1-p. If π is the stationary law, then the complete-state probability is Π_{n,p}:=π([n])=∏_{r=1}^n [rα^r/(n-(n-r)α^r)]. Equivalently, R_{n,p}:=Π_{n,p}^{-1}=∏_{r=1}^n [1+(n/r)(α^{-r}-1)].
results.proof_sketch: The finite chain is irreducible and aperiodic. For a fixed r-set A, let M_r=Pr_π(A⊆S), with M_0=1. For A to be present after one transition, all its coupons must survive, and before losses either A was already present or exactly one member i was absent and the new draw was i. By symmetry, stationarity gives M_r=α^r[(1-r/n)M_r+(r/n)M_{r-1}]. Hence M_r/M_{r-1}=rα^r/[n-(n-r)α^r]. Multiplication gives M_n=Π_{n,p}, since the only n-set is [n]. Dividing each factor into its denominator yields the displayed expression for R_{n,p}.

results.claim: Finite-n hitting-time sandwich. Let H_n=∑_{j=1}^n 1/j and A_{n,p}:=(R_{n,p}-1)/(1-α^n). Then for every n and 0<p<1, A_{n,p}≤E[T_{n,p}]≤H_n A_{n,p}.
results.proof_sketch:
Write h_k for the mean time to hit n from size k and e_k=h_k-h_{k+1}; upward jumps have size at most one, so e_k is the mean passage time from k to k+1 and h_0=∑e_k. Adjacent size chains can be coupled so that their sizes always differ by 0 or 1: couple the indicators that the draw is new monotonically, then couple the common survival trials. Therefore e_0≤e_1≤⋯≤e_{n-1}.

A first-step calculation gives u_ke_k=1+∑_{r<k}e_rF_k(r), where u_k=(n-k)α^{k+1}/n and F_k(r)=Pr(K_1≤r|K_0=k). The adjacent coupling implies ∑_{r=j}^{k-1}F_k(r)≥∑_{r=j}^{k-2}F_{k-1}(r). Abel summation, using that the e_r are increasing, then shows (n-k)e_k is increasing in k. Consequently e_k≤e_{n-1}/(n-k), so h_0≤H_ne_{n-1}.

Kac’s return identity at n and K_1∼Bin(n,α) give R_{n,p}=1+∑_{k<n}Pr_n(K_1=k)h_k. After division by 1-α^n, A_{n,p} is a convex combination of h_0,…,h_{n-1}. Thus e_{n-1}=h_{n-1}≤A_{n,p}≤h_0. Combining these inequalities proves the sandwich.

results.claim: Asymptotic closure throughout the non-classical range. For every fixed η>0, uniformly over η(log n)/n²≤p_n<1, E[T_{n,p_n}]=(1+o(1))A_{n,p_n}=(1+o(1))(R_{n,p_n}-1)/(1-(1-p_n)^n).
results.proof_sketch:
The first-step recurrence also yields e_k/e_{k-1}≥F_k(k-1)/u_k≥k(1-α^k)/[(n-k)α^{k+1}], using the event that an already-held coupon is drawn and at least one coupon is lost. Let m=⌊n/2⌋ and β=m(1-α^m). For k=n-j≥m this ratio is at least β/j. The assumed lower bound on p implies β=Ω_η(log n): if mp≤1, then 1-α^m≥1-e^{-mp}≥mp/2; if mp>1, β=Ω(n).

Set a_j=e_{n-j}/e_{n-1} and J=⌊β/2⌋. For j≤J, a_{j+1}≤(j/β)a_j, hence ∑_{j=2}^J a_j=O(1/β) and a_J≤β^{-1}2^{-J+2}. For j≥J, monotonicity of (n-k)e_k gives a_j≤Ja_J/j. Thus ∑_{j≥J}a_j≤Ja_J(1+log(n/J))=o(1). Therefore h_0/e_{n-1}=∑_{j=1}^n a_j=1+o(1). Since the Kac quantity A_{n,p} lies between e_{n-1} and h_0, all three quantities are asymptotic.

results.claim: The resulting regimes differ from the product-of-marginals prediction. (i) If p=γ(log n)/n² with fixed γ>0, then E[T_{n,p}]∼n^{γ+1}/(γ log n). (ii) If (log n)/n²≪p≪1/n, then log E[T_{n,p}]∼n²p. (iii) If p=c/n with fixed c>0, then n^{-1}log E[T_{n,p}]→I(c):=∫_0^1 log(1+(e^{cx}-1)/x)dx>log(1+c). (iv) If np→∞, then log E[T_{n,p}]∼(n²/2)log(1/(1-p)).
results.proof_sketch:
Let L=log R_{n,p}. Uniformly for p=o(1/n), expansion of α^{-r} gives L=n²p+O(n³p²). At p=γ(log n)/n² this yields R∼n^γ and 1-α^n∼γ(log n)/n, proving (i); together with the exact asymptotic formula it also gives (ii).

For p=c/n, the sum defining L is a Riemann sum, so L/n→I(c). Since e^{cx}-1>cx for x>0, the integrand is strictly larger than log(1+c) away from zero, proving the strict inequality and (iii). In contrast, q*^{-n} has exponential rate log(1+c).

Finally put ℓ=-log α. The product can be rewritten as L=[n(n+1)/2]ℓ+nlog n-log(n!)+∑_{r=1}^n log(1-(1-r/n)e^{-rℓ}). The last sum has absolute value at most ∑_{r≥1}-log(1-e^{-rℓ})≤C/ℓ, by comparison with the finite integral of -log(1-e^{-x}). Thus L=[n(n+1)/2]ℓ+O(n+1/ℓ). When np→∞, nℓ→∞, so the error is lower order, proving (iv).

final_writeup:
Let α=1-p. The correct rare-event quantity is not q*^n but the exact stationary probability

Π_{n,p}=∏_{r=1}^n rα^r/[n-(n-r)α^r].

Indeed, for a fixed r-subset A, its stationary containment probability M_r satisfies

M_r=α^r[(1-r/n)M_r+(r/n)M_{r-1}],

because at most one missing member of A can be supplied in one round. Iterating this recurrence gives Π_{n,p}=M_n. Write

R_{n,p}=Π_{n,p}^{-1}=∏_{r=1}^n [1+(n/r)(α^{-r}-1)].

There is also a necessary correction for clustering of visits to the complete state. From [n], the chain remains complete with probability α^n, so complete-state entrances have stationary flux Π_{n,p}(1-α^n). Kac’s identity makes this precise. If h_k is the expected hitting time from k coupons, then

R_{n,p}=1+∑_{k<n}Pr(Bin(n,α)=k)h_k.

Consequently

A_{n,p}:=(R_{n,p}-1)/(1-α^n)

is a convex combination of h_0,…,h_{n-1} conditional on leaving n.

To compare these hitting times, define e_k=h_k-h_{k+1}, the expected time required to pass from level k to k+1. A monotone adjacent-state coupling proves that e_k is increasing. A first-step recurrence plus Abel summation strengthens this to monotonicity of (n-k)e_k. Hence

h_0=∑_{k=0}^{n-1}e_k≤e_{n-1}H_n.

Since h_{n-1}=e_{n-1}≤A_{n,p}≤h_0, this gives the exact finite bound

A_{n,p}≤E[T_{n,p}]≤H_nA_{n,p}.

More is true in every non-classical regime. The first-step recurrence implies

e_k/e_{k-1}≥k(1-α^k)/[(n-k)α^{k+1}].

For p≥η(log n)/n², these ratios force the final passage e_{n-1} to dominate the sum of all earlier passages. Quantitatively, with m=⌊n/2⌋ and β=m(1-α^m)=Ω_η(log n), the normalized earlier passages have a geometrically decreasing initial segment and, using monotonicity of (n-k)e_k, a vanishing harmonic tail. Thus h_0/e_{n-1}→1. Since A_{n,p} lies between them,

E[T_{n,p}]=(1+o(1))(R_{n,p}-1)/(1-(1-p)^n),

uniformly for every fixed η>0 and η(log n)/n²≤p<1. This closes the hitting-time asymptotics in all recorded non-classical regimes.

The formula also shows that the proposed lower/mean-field scale is not generally tight. At p=γ(log n)/n²,

E[T_{n,p}]∼n^{γ+1}/(γlog n),

rather than q*^{-n}∼n^γ. When p=c/n, the true exponential rate is

I(c)=∫_0^1 log(1+(e^{cx}-1)/x)dx,

which is strictly larger than log(1+c), the q*^{-n} rate. Finally, for np→∞,

log E[T_{n,p}]∼(n²/2)log(1/(1-p));

for fixed p this is Θ(n²), versus only Θ(nlog n) in the product-of-marginals prediction. The discrepancy comes from both spatial negative dependence and temporal clustering at the complete state.
checks_performed: Read only the designated JSON input; no web access or other repository files were used.

Constructed the reduced transition matrix with exact rational arithmetic for all n=1,…,8 and p∈{1/11,2/5,4/5}. Across all 24 instances, exact Gaussian elimination verified the stationary product, Kac identity, monotonicity of e_k and (n-k)e_k, and both sides of the finite sandwich.

Symbolically solved the exact hitting equations for n≤5 and checked that their factorizations agree with the stationary and passage-time identities. High-precision recurrence evaluations at critical and metastable scalings were additionally used as sanity checks.
